title: This Fish Makes 600 Volts. How? ⚡
description:
How does an electric eel make 600 volts? Most of its body is an electric organ made of thousands of cells called electrocytes, each making a tiny charge, stacked head to tail like batteries in a flashlight so one nerve signal fires them all at once into a single big shock.

topic: How does an electric eel make 600 volts?
script: An electric eel can zap you with 600 volts. But how? That's five times your wall outlet, and there's no battery inside. Its body is the battery. Most of that long body is packed with special cells called electrocytes. Each one makes a tiny charge, less than a fifth of a volt. Alone, that's nothing. But they're stacked in rows, thousands of them, head to tail, like batteries in a flashlight. When the eel spots a fish, its brain fires one signal, and every cell flips on at once. About six thousand tiny charges add up to one giant shock. Zap! The fish freezes on the spot. Here's the twist: an electric eel isn't even an eel. It's a knifefish, closer to a catfish. So if your body were a battery, what would you power first?
key_facts: The shock comes from the Main and Hunter's organs: some 5,000 to 6,000 stacked electroplaques (electrocytes), working like a battery (Fluke); script says 'about six thousand'
Each electrocyte makes only about 0.15 volt (Fluke); script says 'less than a fifth of a volt', screen shows 0.15 V
A motor-neuron signal opens ion channels so each cell becomes a dipole, and many cells firing together add up to a strong shock (Science ABC)
Electric eels reach about 600 volts (Fluke: up to 500 V; record before 2019 was 650 V; E. voltai measured 860 V, FAPESP); US wall outlet is 120 V, so 600 V = 5x
The electric organ fills most of the body (about two-thirds per Science ABC; script says 'most of that long body')
Electric eels are not true eels: they are knifefishes, more closely related to catfish and carp (FAPESP, Science ABC)
